name: Aragonese
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand sources agree (0 agree, 2 refine), none contradicts
catalog_citation: Mott, Brian. 2007. Chistabino (Pyrenean Aragonese). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 37(1): 103-114. doi:10.1017/S0025100306002842
catalog_locator: p. 110 (PDF p. 8 of 12), section 'Prosody' > 'Lexical stress'; file, page image
catalog_quote: Words in Chistabino are usually stressed on the penultimate or final syllable, as in all Aragonese accents: desenfaixa [deseɱˈfai̯ʃa] ‘s/he undoes the bundle of grass’, desenfaixar [deseɱfai̯ˈʃa] ‘to undo a bundle of grass’. Antepenultimate stress is much rarer than in Spanish, though you sometimes find hypercorrect forms like pántano [ˈpan̪tano] ‘reservoir’ (Spanish pantano [pan̪ˈtano]). In third person imperatives, the antepenultimate stress of Spanish is avoided by the fact that the reflexive pronoun precedes the verb: s’asiente usté [saˈsjen̪te usˈte], s’asienten ustés [saˈsjen̪ten usˈtes] ‘sit down’ (cf. Spanish siéntese usted, siéntense ustedes).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Romance-type lexical/morphological stress confined in practice to the last two syllables: penultimate or final depending on the word (e.g. verb form desenfáixa vs infinitive desenfaixár); antepenultimate stress is marginal (rarer than in Spanish, avoided/regularised to penultimate), so stress is not predictable from a single fixed position but falls within a final two-(three-)syllable window. Corroborated by EFA 2017 Gramatica Basica sec. 1.2.1.1 (agudas/planas/esdruixolas; 'l'aragonés gosa refusar las parolas esdruixolas, tornando-las en planas') and AAL 2023 Ortografía 3.2c/4.3.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mott says nothing on secondary stress. AAL 2023 Ortografía 3.5c: adverbs in -ment are final-stressed and 'pueden presentar un acento secundario en o lexema' (may carry a secondary accent on the lexical base).
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress rare (hypercorrect pántano; toponyms per EFA 2017; habitual in some varieties such as ansotano per AAL 2023 3.2c); learned proparoxytones adapted as paroxytones (grafico, medico). Phrase-final unstressed syllables, especially south of Huesca and in the Ebro Valley, may be lengthened with a pitch rise, giving an impression of stress displacement (less noticeable in Chistabino).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress; Mott separately describes phrase-level prominence (final-syllable lengthening/pitch rise in intonation units) and states the nuclear tone falls on the last stressed syllable of the intonation phrase (p.111). Description is of the Chistabino (Gistaín valley) dialect but the stress statement is explicitly generalised to 'all Aragonese accents'.
new_statements.identity_note: Mott 2007 describes Chistabino, the Aragonese of the Gistaín (Chistau) valley, Huesca (speakers from Gistaín/Serveto); no separate Glottolog code known to me under arag1245 for this variety. The stress sentence is explicitly generalised by the author to 'all Aragonese accents', and the EFA 2017 grammar and AAL 2023 orthography (both for standard/common Aragonese) agree: final or penultimate stress, proparoxytones rare and regularised to penultimate (except e.g. ansotano and toponyms).

new_statements.quote: Dabei ist die vorletzte Wortsilbe, wohl wegen der auf der iberischen Halbinsel überwiegenden Zahl der existierenden Paroxytona, für den Hauptton die bevorzugte. So ergeben sich etwa die folgenden Tonverlagerungen : ítamela : itaméla Hecho, pósate : posáte Loarre, águila : aɣíla Loarre, [p. 239] báscula : baskúla Hecho, calorífero : kalóriféro Fablo, cáñamo : kañámo Ansó, sonst allg. kañímo, pájaro : pašáro, paɣáro Loarre. Eine stark beschleunigende Wirkung in dieser Hinsicht hat die Analogie der Suffixe [...] ácido : aθ-íðo Hecho, púlpito : pulp-íto ib., [...] música : mus-íka Hecho [...]. (p. 184:) -ĭcus [...], urspr. Adjektiva bildend, hat seinen Akzent auf die bevorzugte vorletzte Silbe gelegt und damit die Wörter zu Paroxytonen gemacht wie ja alle span. Suffixe.
new_statements.translation: In this the penultimate syllable of the word, probably because of the preponderant number of existing paroxytones on the Iberian Peninsula, is the preferred one for the main stress. Thus arise for instance the following stress shifts: ítamela : itaméla Hecho, pósate : posáte Loarre, águila : aɣíla Loarre, báscula : baskúla Hecho, calorífero : kalóriféro Fablo, cáñamo : kañámo Ansó, otherwise generally kañímo, pájaro : pašáro, paɣáro Loarre. A strongly accelerating effect in this respect is exerted by the analogy of the suffixes [...] ácido : aθ-íðo Hecho, púlpito : pulp-íto ib., [...] música : mus-íka Hecho [...]. (p. 184:) -ĭcus [...], originally forming adjectives, has placed its accent on the favoured penultimate syllable and thereby made the words paroxytones, as indeed all Spanish suffixes do.

So ergeben sich etwa die folgenden Tonverlagerungen: itamela : itamela Hecho, posate : posate Loarre, aguila : a[gamma]ila Loarre,' continuing on p.239 'bascula : baskula Hecho, calorifero : kaloriféro Fablo, cáñamo : kañámo Ansó, sonst…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Mott 2007 statement for Chistabino ('penultimate or final syllable, as in all Aragonese accents; antepenultimate stress is much rarer than in Spanish'): Kuhn supplies the mechanism and evidence for that rarity, namely the systematic shift of Spanish proparoxytones to paroxytones across the High Aragonese villages (Ansó, Hecho, Aragüés, Embún, Loarre, Fablo, Ypiés, Biescas, Fiscal), plus the statement that the penult is the preferred position of main stress. It adds no different placement and does not contradict the catalog (whose rule field is empty).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kuhn gives no rule of the form 'stress falls on syllable X'; his only explicit statement on stress placement (sec. 109, framed as a historical/dialectological remark on 'Akzentverlegung') is that the penult is the preferred position for main stress in High Aragonese, so that Spanish proparoxytones are regularly re-stressed as paroxytones (águila > aɣíla, báscula > baskúla, cáñamo > kañímo, pájaro > payáro, música > musíka, ácido > aθíðo), often via reinterpretation of the ending as a stressed suffix (-íto, -íko, -áno, -ín); oxytones with stressed suffixes (-ón, -ín, -ál, -ár) and words with apocope (fray < fraxinus, sec. 15 p. 53) are abundant, so stress remains lexically distributed between final and penult with antepenultimate stress largely eliminated. The Lautlehre (part 1) has no accent section; the only stress-related section there is sec. 31 'Unbetonte Vokale' (p. 110), on vowel changes in unstressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. (Kuhn transcribes a secondary/grave accent in a few polysyllables, e.g. mòrθyal-áɣo Loarre, àlikaŋk-áno Embún, èstom-áɣo Hecho, p. 239, without comment.)
new_statements.exceptions: Village-specific variation: cáñamo is kañámo in Ansó but kañímo elsewhere; murciélago gives mòrθyaláɣo Loarre / mùrθyaláɣo and mùrθyaɣálo Ypiés; esteba > esteβán Bolea vs estéβan Fablo, Aineto, Loarre, Huesca (p. 240); p. 149 notes Embún/Aineto retract the stress of 1st/2nd pl. subjunctive fáyyamos onto the stem by analogy with the stem-stressed present, unlike Ansó, Hecho, Panticosa, Torla (fayámos); p. 127-128 notes proparoxytone verb forms in -nos (éranos, ésenos 'habíamos, hubiésemos', Hecho, Torla).
new_statements.identity_note: Kuhn 1935 describes 'Hocharagonesisch' (High/Upper Aragonese) from fieldwork in the Pyrenean valleys and foothills of Huesca: chiefly Ansó, Hecho, Aragüés, Embún, Panticosa, Lanuza, Biescas, Torla, Fiscal, Fablo, Aineto, Ypiés, Bolea, Loarre (principal informant for Hecho: Veremundo Méndez, p. 6). His stress examples are tagged by village; the Gistaín/Chistabino variety of Mott 2007 is not among his points. The p. 184 remark on -icus is a general statement about Spanish/Ibero-Romance suffixes, applied to Aragonese forms.

sources.note: Sec. 1.2.1.1 (printed pp.3-4, PDF pp.41-42): polysyllabic words have one stressed syllable; agudas (final), planas (penultimate), esdruixolas (antepenultimate); proparoxytones 'no son guaire comuns en aragonés, ya que l'aragonés gosa refusar las parolas esdruixolas, tornando-las en planas', though found in toponymy. Sec. 1.4.1 gives written-accent rules.

sources.citation: Academia Aragonesa de la Lengua. 2023. Ortografía de l'aragonés. Zaragoza. 29 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Ch.3 (PDF p.13): accent-mark rules by agudas/planas/esdruixulas; where pronunciation vacillates between plana and esdruixula the plana form is recommended 'seguindo la tendencia prosodica de l'aragonés moderno: grafico, medico', but in varieties like ansotano proparoxytone pronunciation is habitual; adverbs in -ment are agudas with a possible secondary accent on the lexeme (3.5c). Sec. 4.3 (PDF p.15): Greek/Latin proparoxytone cultismos are adapted as paroxytones in modern Aragonese.
